item.title: National water shortage officially over but troubles continue
item.description:
National water shortage officially over but troubles continue

September 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Netherlands is officially out of a water shortage, but the drought that left houseboats stranded and cargo barges part-loaded throughout the summer will be felt for months to come, the infrastructure ministry has said.

Weeks of rain and falling demand have allowed the ministry to move the country from level two to level one on its three-stage scale of water shortages – from an actual shortage back to an impending one. Crops are being harvested, farmers are irrigating less and cooler weather means less water is evaporating.

The government team that met weekly through the summer to tackle the shortage will now disband, though the national water distribution committee, which warned of serious water shortages in July, will keep meeting, and the weekly drought monitor continues.

Recovery will take months
The downgrade does not mean the drought is over. The Rhine is still carrying only about half its normal volume for early September and river levels could stay low until the end of the year. Groundwater will also take even longer to get back to normal levels.

For the houseboat owners stranded on stretches of the Rhine that dried up months ago, there will be little immediate relief. Their homes will not refloat until levels rise. Shipping also faces reduced services and delays at locks.

Water abstraction restrictions still apply across the higher sandy soils of the east and south, and salinisation of the IJsselmeer remains a concern for drinking water suppliers, though some water boards have begun rolling back restrictions. Drinking water supplies remain secure.

item.title: Inspectors allow only Dutch online abortion service to continue
item.description:
Inspectors allow only Dutch online abortion service to continue

September 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch’ healthcare inspectorate has found that the country’s only online abortion service fell short on its duties for care, but will let it keep operating after the site agreed to change its practices.

Thuisabortus.nl, which launched in March, was the first service in the Netherlands to let women get the abortion pill prescribed without an in-person visit to a GP or clinic.

The inspectorate, the IGJ, said the main problem was that women who ordered the pill through the website usually had no personal contact with a doctor before it was prescribed but it also found no serious risk to patients and so no reason to shut it down.

As a remedial measure, the site has since telephoned every woman who applies, discussing the stage of the pregnancy, possible complications, aftercare through her own GP and alternatives to abortion.

Concerns raised at launch
When the site was launched, the family doctors organisation KNMG and the GP organisation LHV questioned whether issuing the pill without a consultation met the legal duty of care.

Health minister Sophie Hermans told MPs on Wednesday that the government regretted the shortcomings, and described the conversation between a woman and her doctor as an “essential part” of careful abortion care.

The site’s founder, GP Peter Leusink, said he would comply but disagreed, arguing that a phone consultation is not needed for safe care and pointing to home use of the pill in the US, the UK and Sweden. “We have to comply with that outdated law,” he told NRC.

Doctors remain divided
The abortion doctors’ association NGvA said the report confirmed its concern that the platform had started in a hurry and overlooked parts of proper care, and that it was now exploring a digital service of its own. The GPs’ professional body NHG has backed online abortion care as a useful addition and called for GPs and the site to work together.

The LHV said it still had concerns about who handles complications at night and at weekends. The orthodox Protestant SGP and the ChristenUnie went further, with SGP MP Diederik van Dijk saying the service should have been taken offline.

GPs have been able to prescribe the abortion pill since the start of 2025, after completing extra training. Thuisabortus.nl says it has prescribed around 1,680 pills since April, about a quarter of all abortion pills issued in the Netherlands. The inspectorate has given the site until mid-November to complete the remaining changes.

item.title: Illegal casinos hijack thousands of Dutch websites
item.description:
Illegal casinos hijack thousands of Dutch websites

September 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

At least 1,000 legitimate Dutch and European websites, many belonging to companies, charities and freelancers, have been quietly turned into shopfronts for illegal online casinos, an investigation by radio station BNR has found. The real figure might be over 8,000.

The sites have nothing to do with gambling, and their owners are usually unaware. Criminals either hack poorly secured websites and add casino pages, or buy up an organisation’s expired domain name and fill it with gambling content.

Because search engines already trust those addresses, the casino pages rank highly. Someone searching for an online casino may land on a seemingly reputable site before being redirected to an illegal operator.

BNR found gambling pages on an old domain once used by broadcaster and writer Wilfried de Jong, on sites formerly run by the liberal VVD party in Zeeland and Brabant, and on the website of a business lawyer, where at least 50 casino pages had been added.

The national gambling authority called it “a very big problem” and is working with SIDN, the body that manages Dutch internet domains, to shut down redirect pages, but the process is slow because there is no legal power to block the sites, which SIDN says it wants.

It can also do little about .com or .eu addresses, which fall outside SIDN’s remit, so it is hoping Google will step in. The search engine removes adverts for illegal casinos but leaves the sites and redirect pages in place.

The cabinet said in June it was drawing up new tools with the authority to tackle illegal gambling, including the power to block websites. Regulators have struggled to keep up, with more now being spent on illegal sites in the Netherlands than on legal ones.

item.title: Minister given permission to axe far-right TV broadcaster
item.description:
Minister given permission to axe far-right TV broadcaster

September 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Netherlands’ media minister, Rianne Letschert, has obtained the legal authority to strip the far-right broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland (ON) of its licence, meaning it could be taken off air from public broadcasting and lose its public funding.

The Dutch media authority set out a case in a letter to Letschert, weeks after ON presenters spoke of their approval and agreements with certain Adolf Hitler remarks in a July broadcast.

It called the show a turning point and said it no longer trusted ON to run its operations properly.

Letschert has said a licence can only be withdrawn once two formal sanctions are in place, both of which have now been fulfilled. The first was a fine imposed last September for conflict-of-interest breaches and for ignoring editorial rules, and a separate penalty order for withholding records of how it spent public money.

ON director Peter Vlemmix told the ANP news agency the broadcaster would continue its “fight for survival” and accused the authority of overlooking improvements made over the past year.

Letschert has promised to tell MPs her decision on ON’s future before a parliamentary debate on September 24.

item.title: Court orders release of euthanasia letter signatories
item.description:
Court orders release of euthanasia letter signatories

September 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A court in The Hague ruled on Thursday that the public prosecution service (OM) must hand over the names the 14 prominent doctors who signed a letter urging an investigation into the case of Milou, a 17-year-old died by euthanasia in 2023.

Her parents, who were subjected to death threats after the letter was leaked, sued to obtain the names of the medical professionals who penned the later.

The OM had refused to provide the names, six of which are already known, citing privacy concerns.

Judges in The Hague said that it was “unreasonable to refuse to provide the letter containing names to the parents” who have a “compelling interest” in the information.

The parents could choose to pursue disciplinary or civil legal action against the doctors.

Milou had suffered from mental health problems from the age of 11 following sexual abuse. She was again sexually abused in an institution by another patient.

After years of treatment and various suicide attempts, she chose euthanasia at the age of 17 on the grounds of unbearable mental suffering.

The psychiatrist who approved her decision acted in accordance with the guidelines, the regional euthanasia review committee RTE found.

The committee reviews all euthanasia procedures to make sure the correct procedures have been followed and reports back to the OM, which now has five days to hand over the names.

item.title: Student room shortage stays above 20,000 despite new builds
item.description:
Student room shortage stays above 20,000 despite new builds

September 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

More students in the Netherlands are staying in their parents’ home or giving up the search for a place of their own, as the shortage of student housing remains high despite thousands of new rooms being built each year.

The country is short of more than 20,200 student rooms, barely down from 21,000 a year earlier, according to the annual student housing monitor from knowledge centre Kences, published this week.

Social housing providers have built nearly 5,000 units a year since 2022, meeting the targets they were set.

Kences had expected the shortage to climb, because private landlords have been selling up in response to new rent rules and higher taxes. Some 32,300 fewer students have rented from private landlords since 2024.

That did not translate into a sharp rise, largely because student numbers have also dropped, including among international students. The share of students living away from home has fallen from 50% to 43% over eight years.

Fewer rooms, riskier ads
The rooms still on the private market are increasingly hard to rent safely. Many are advertised above the legal limit.

Scammers, meanwhile, have flooded TikTok with fake listings that pocket deposits for rooms that do not exist.

Internationals are especially exposed to housing fraud, as they rarely have a family home to fall back on and often do not know their rights.

Kences wants the profit tax paid by housing associations scrapped, which it says would fund 15,000 to 25,000 more student homes over ten years. “Every euro we hand to the tax office, we would rather put into housing,” director Reijnder Jan Spits told broadcaster NOS.

Even if every current building plan goes ahead, the centre warned, the shortage could still stand at between 10,000 and 35,000 rooms in eight years.

item.title: Cybercrime and online fraud hit 2.5 million people in 2025
item.description:
Cybercrime and online fraud hit 2.5 million people in 2025

September 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

An estimated 2.5 million people in the Netherlands fell victim to cybercrime or an online form of fraud, deception or intimidation last year, according to a new report by prosecutors and police that warns the threat is becoming harder to contain.

The Cybercrimebeeld Nederland, published every two years by the public prosecution department (OM) and the Dutch police, says offenders are increasingly working across borders and paying for whatever expertise they lack.

Technical skill is now widely for sale, the report says: ready-made tools, stolen data and services allow novice hackers to create complex attacks.

“Criminals combine data from earlier hacks with newly stolen data,” said Christa de Pagter, the national public prosecutor for cybercrime. Offenders use it to make more targetted attacks on victims, she said, often posing as a bank or crypto platform to pressure them into acting.

State actors blur the line
The report also revealed the growing role of state actors, which it says are increasingly entangled with criminal groups through hybrid warfare, eroding the line between cybercrime and national security. States can use criminals as proxies, directing them or supplying money and infrastructure.

In May, Dutch investigators arrested two men over servers used for Russian-linked cyberattacks; the report also cites two 17-year-olds detained last year for mapping wifi networks around government buildings in The Hague.

Lured through online games
Prosecutors and police also describe a new generation of young, Western cybercriminals, driven by money and status rather than ideology, who meet in loose online networks and specialise in data and cryptocurrency theft. They range in age from 11 to 25, police cybercrime lead Stan Duijf told broadcaster NOS.

Children are often lured in through online games such as Roblox, Fortnite and Minecraft, where they can be groomed in chat rooms. “It’s just like the schoolyard: they start with mischief,” Duijf said – but some go on to become cybercriminals.

The report highlights this year’s hack on Odido, which police believe a Dutch gang using the name ShinyHunters carried out, exposing the data of 6.2 million customers and prompting a €1 million ransom demand the firm refused.

AI is described as a “catalyst”: the report says it does not fundamentally change cybercrime but increases its speed and scale, and makes scam emails harder to spot.

item.title: Rabbit farms face prosecution over abuse footage
item.description:
Rabbit farms face prosecution over abuse footage

September 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Sixteen Dutch rabbit farms could face criminal prosecution after undercover footage showed bunnies being lifted by the ears and thrown into crates, and sick animals beaten to death, junior agriculture minister Silvio Erkens has said.

The images, filmed by campaign group Animal Rights, were shot at 16 companies that export live rabbits to slaughterhouses in Belgium. They show the animals being picked up by the ears, fur, legs or head and thrown in large numbers into transport crates and shopping trolleys, where they can be crushed.

“What can be seen in the footage is terrible,” Erkens said in answer to parliamentary questions from D66 and the animal rights party PvdD, calling the treatment unacceptable. Some people, he added, appeared to feel free to handle animals this way when no inspector was nearby.

The food safety board NVWA has received a large amount of recent footage and is checking it for authenticity. If abuse is found companies are prosecuted. In 2024 a slaughterhouse was fined for cruelty after activists released undercover video.

Footage seen so far points to structural and serious failings in how the animals are handled, Erkens said. He has also set up new checks on how rabbits are caught and loaded – a stage of animal transport that inspections had largely overlooked, and will update parliament by the end of the year.

item.title: Dutch swimming water increasingly polluted, researchers find
item.description:
Dutch swimming water increasingly polluted, researchers find

September 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Swimming water in the Netherlands is still often polluted with chemicals and bacteria, according to new research by an environmental group and The Netherlands Institute for Ecology.

The researchers investigated the water quality from 205 official swimming locations and 57 other popular urban swimming spots

They were looking for 122 pollutants and found excess quantities of 35 substances in ponds, rivers and lakes around the country.

According the report, the number of locations with pollution rising. In particular incidents of blue-green algae have gone up in the past five years.

Water quality testing in the Netherlands focuses primarily on contaminants that cause acute health risks like blue-green algae and E. coli, and doesn’t include industrial substances and pesticides.

The group is calling for for stricter licensing of waste water disposal and increased monitoring of bathing waters.

item.title: Little help for girls in NL caught up in crime: study
item.description:
Little help for girls in NL caught up in crime: study

September 3, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

There is very little help for girls and young women who get caught up in the Dutch criminal justice system, a new government-backed study has found. The findings show the majority of treatment options are aimed at boys, who have different needs and problems.

The study is by the justice ministry’s research centre WODC and Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. They looked at 22 international treatment methods for young female criminal offenders.

Only one such method is studied, used and seen as promising for girls in the Netherlands: a treatment that helps them manage aggression. For most other kinds of help, it is simply not known whether they do any good.

Different problems
Most programmes are built around boys, who make up the majority of young offenders. But girls and young women usually end up in the system for different reasons.

Their behaviour more often traces back to issues such as anxiety, trouble with their parents, or sexual abuse. Boys are more likely to struggle with aggression, poor self-control, or falling in with the wrong crowd.

Because of that, help designed for boys does not always help girls – especially the lighter support given at home or through youth care.

Divided opinions
Not all experts and researchers agree this is a problem. Some say programmes are always tailored to the individual anyway, so they work for boys and girls alike. Others want clearer guidance for working with girls.

Girls and young women are behind only a small share of recorded crime, usually less serious, such as theft.

Among the youngest, under 16, there has been a slight rise in violent offences. Why is not clear. It follows a wider rise in teen crime recorded last year.
